quotes.text: A password is a shared secret because you and the server both know it. Anything that two parties share can be copied by either one of them.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Explains in two sentences why shared secrets are the core weakness of passwords.

quotes.text: the pin is not the secret that protects your account. It's what unlocks the key that protects your account, and that key stays on the machine.
quotes.speaker: Mirko Peters
quotes.why: Clears up the common misconception that a short PIN is weaker than a long password.

quotes.text: The private half is the sensitive one, and it's created inside the chip and can't be exported, which means there's no file anyone can copy off your machine.

takeaways: Windows Hello for Business replaces the shared-secret password with a key pair whose private half is created in the TPM and never leaves the device.
A short PIN can beat a long password because it only works on one device, is never sent to a server and is protected by hardware against guessing.
Key trust, certificate trust and cloud Kerberos trust differ in required infrastructure, not in security, and Microsoft recommends cloud Kerberos trust for typical hybrid setups.
hook: Passwords get reused, phished and stolen, and even MFA still leaves them in the picture. This Simply Explained episode shows end users and IT beginners how Windows Hello for Business, the TPM and device-bound keys take the password out of the sign-in and why a four-digit PIN can be safer than a fourteen-character password.
